column2: Answering him, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all the people,
3	truly this is a fair thing, to listen to a singer
4	such as this one is, like the gods in voice.
5	For I say there is no more gracious end
6	than when cheer holds the whole people,
7	and banqueters through the house listen to a singer
8	sitting in rows, and beside them tables are laden
9	with bread and meat, and the wine-bearer, drawing wine from the mixing-bowl,
10	carries it round and pours it into the cups;
11	this seems to me in my mind to be the fairest thing.
12	But your heart has turned to ask about my sorrowful cares,
13	that I may groan still more in lamenting.
14	What first then shall I tell you, and what last?
15	For the heavenly gods have given me many cares.
16	Now first I will tell my name, that you too may
17	know it, and that I, escaping the pitiless day,
18	may be your guest, though I live in a house far away.
19	I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, who for all kinds of tricks
20	am a concern to men, and my fame reaches heaven.
21	I live in sunny Ithaca; on it is a mountain,
22	Neritum, covered with rustling leaves, conspicuous; and around it islands
23	many lie very near to one another,
24	Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus.
25	It itself lies low, farthest up in the sea
26	toward the dusk, while the others are apart toward the dawn and the sun,
27	rugged, but a good nurse of young men; for I
28	can see nothing sweeter than one's own land.
29	Indeed Calypso, bright among goddesses, kept me there
30	in her hollow caves, longing for me to be her husband;
31	and in the same way Circe held me back in her halls,
32	the crafty Aeaean, longing for me to be her husband;
33	but they never persuaded my heart in my breast.
34	So nothing is sweeter than one's own country and parents,
35	even if one lives in a rich house
36	in a foreign land, far from one's parents.
37	But come, let me tell you of my much-troubled return,
38	which Zeus laid on me as I came from Troy.
39	From Ilios the wind carried me and brought me near the Cicones,
40	to Ismarus. There I sacked the city, and destroyed the men;
41	and from the city taking wives and many possessions
42	we divided them, that none might go off cheated of an equal share.
43	There I indeed bade us flee with nimble foot,
44	but they, greatly foolish, did not obey.
45	There much wine was drunk, and many sheep
46	they slaughtered on the shore, and shambling, crook-horned cattle.
47	Meanwhile the Cicones went and called to other Cicones,
48	who were their neighbours, more numerous and better men,
49	living on the mainland, skilled at fighting
50	against men from horses and, where need was, on foot.
51	They came then as many as the leaves and flowers that grow in season,
52	in the morning; then the evil fate of Zeus stood by
53	us ill-fated men, that we might suffer many pains.
54	They took their stand and fought a battle beside the swift ships,
55	and struck one another with bronze-tipped spears.
56	As long as it was morning and the sacred day grew,
57	so long we held our ground and warded them off, though they were more.
58	But when the sun moved toward the time of unyoking oxen,
59	then the Cicones, having overcome the Achaeans, turned them.
60	Six well-greaved companions from each ship
61	perished; and the rest of us escaped death and fate.
62	From there we sailed on, grieved at heart,
63	glad to escape death, having lost our dear companions.
64	Nor did my curved ships go on
65	before we had called three times on each of the wretched companions
66	who died on the plain, slain by the Cicones.
67	And on the ships Zeus the cloud-gatherer roused the North Wind
68	with a marvellous squall, and covered with clouds
69	land and sea together; and night rushed down from heaven.
70	Then the ships were carried headlong, and their sails
71	the force of the wind tore in three and four pieces.
72	These we lowered into the ships, fearing destruction,
73	and rowed the ships eagerly on toward the mainland.
74	There two nights and two days continuously
75	we lay, eating our hearts together with weariness and pains.
76	But when fair-tressed Dawn brought the third day to its end,
77	setting the masts and hauling up the white sails
78	we sat, and wind and helmsmen steered the ships.
79	And now I would have come unharmed to my native land;
80	but the wave and current as I rounded Malea
81	and the North Wind drove me off, and swept me past Cythera.
82	From there for nine days I was carried by baleful winds
83	over the fishy sea; but on the tenth we set foot
84	on the land of the Lotus-eaters, who eat a flowery food.
85	There we stepped on the mainland and drew water,
86	and quickly my companions took a meal beside the swift ships.
87	But when we had tasted food and drink,
88	then I sent companions ahead to go and find out
89	who the men were that eat bread on this land,
90	choosing two men, and sending a herald as a third with them.
91	and they, going quickly, mingled with the Lotus-eating men;
92	nor did the Lotus-eaters plan destruction for my
93	companions, but gave them some of the lotus to eat.
94	And whoever of them ate the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus
95	no longer wished to bring back word or to return,
96	but wished to stay there among the Lotus-eating men
97	feeding on lotus and to forget their homecoming.
98	These I brought back to the ships, weeping, by force,
99	and in the hollow ships I dragged them and bound them under the benches.
100	And the other trusty companions I bade
101	to hasten and go aboard the swift ships,
102	lest some, eating lotus, forget their homecoming.
103	They quickly embarked and sat on the benches,
104	and sitting in order they struck the grey sea with oars.
105	From there we sailed on, grieved at heart;
106	and we came to the land of the Cyclopes, overweening and lawless,
107	who, trusting in the immortal gods,
108	neither plant a plant with their hands nor plough,
109	but all these things grow unsown and unploughed,
110	wheat and barley and vines, which bear
111	wine from rich clusters, and the rain of Zeus makes them grow.
112	They have neither assemblies for counsel nor laws,
113	but they dwell on the peaks of high mountains
114	in hollow caves, and each lays down the law
115	to his children and wives, and they care nothing for one another.
116	Then an island, level, stretches along outside the harbour,
117	of the land of the Cyclopes, neither near nor far away,
118	wooded; and on it are goats without number,
119	wild; for no tread of men scares them off,
120	nor do hunters go in, who in the forest
121	suffer hardships following the peaks of the mountains.
122	It is held neither by flocks nor by ploughing,
123	but unsown and unploughed all its days
124	it is empty of men, and feeds bleating goats.
125	For the Cyclopes have no vermilion-cheeked ships,
126	nor are there shipwrights among them, who could build
127	well-benched ships, which would accomplish everything,
128	going to the cities of men, such as men often
129	cross the sea in ships to visit one another;
130	who would also have made the island a well-settled place for them.
131	For it is by no means bad, and would bear everything in season;
132	for there are meadows along the shores of the grey sea,
133	watery and soft; the vines would be unfailing.
134	There is smooth ploughland; a deep harvest always
135	they would reap in season, since it is very rich beneath the soil.
136	And there is a harbour with good anchorage, where there is no need of cable,
137	neither to throw anchor-stones nor to tie stern cables,
138	but to run ashore and wait a time until the sailors'
139	spirit urges and the breezes blow.
140	And at the head of the harbour flows bright water,
141	a spring under a cave; and poplars grow around.
142	There we sailed in, and some god led us
143	through the dark night, and it was not visible to see;
144	for there was thick mist around the ships, and the moon
145	did not shine from heaven, but was held by clouds.
146	There no one saw the island with his eyes,
147	nor did we see the long waves rolling toward the shore,
148	before we ran the well-benched ships aground.
149	And when the ships had run aground we lowered all the sails,
150	and went out ourselves onto the shore of the sea;
151	there falling asleep we waited for divine Dawn.
152	When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
153	marvelling at the island we went about through it.
154	And the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, roused
155	mountain goats, that my companions might have a meal.
156	At once we took curved bows and long-socketed javelins
157	from the ships, and, arranged in three bands,
158	we shot; and quickly a god gave us satisfying hunting.
159	Twelve ships followed me, and to each
160	nine goats fell by lot; and for me alone they picked out ten.
161	So then all day until the sun set
162	we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
163	for the red wine had not yet run out from the ships,
164	but was still in them; for each crew had drawn off much
165	in jars from the Cicones, when we took the sacred citadel.
166	And we looked at the land of the Cyclopes, which was near,
167	and at their smoke and the voice of their sheep and goats.
168	When the sun set and darkness came on,
169	then we lay down on the shore of the sea.
170	When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
171	then I called an assembly and spoke among all:
172	You others stay now, my trusty companions;
but I with my ship and my companions
will go and make trial of these men, who they are,
whether they are insolent and savage and unjust,
or hospitable, and their mind is god-fearing."
So saying I went aboard the ship, and bade my companions
to embark themselves and loose the stern cables.
They quickly embarked and sat on the benches,
and sitting in order they struck the grey sea with oars.
But when we reached the place, which was near,
there at the edge we saw a cave near the sea,
high, roofed over with laurels. There many
flocks, sheep and goats, used to sleep; and around it a court
was built high with deep-set stones
and with tall pines and high-leaved oaks.
There a monstrous man used to sleep, who tended the flocks
alone, far off; nor did he go among others,
but, being apart, knew lawless ways.
For he was made a monstrous wonder, nor was he like
a bread-eating man, but like a wooded peak
of high mountains, which appears alone apart from others.
Then I bade the rest of my trusty companions
to stay there by the ship and guard the ship,
and I, choosing twelve of my best companions,
went; and I had a goat-skin of dark wine,
sweet, which Maron gave me, son of Euanthes,
priest of Apollo, who protected Ismarus,
because we had spared him with his child and wife,
out of reverence; for he lived in a wooded grove
of Phoebus Apollo. And he gave me splendid gifts:
he gave me seven talents of well-wrought gold,
and gave me a mixing-bowl all of silver, and then
wine, having drawn it into twelve jars in all,
sweet, unmixed, a divine drink; and none
of the servants or handmaids in his house knew it,
but only himself and his dear wife and one housekeeper.
And whenever they drank that honey-sweet red wine,
filling one cup, twenty measures of water
he poured in, and a sweet smell rose from the mixing-bowl,
marvellous; then it was no pleasure to hold off.
Of this I carried, having filled a great skin, and I took food too
in a bag; for at once my proud spirit suspected
that a man would come upon me, clothed in great strength,
savage, knowing well neither justice nor laws.
Quickly we reached the cave, and did not find him within,
but he was pasturing his fat flocks in the pasture.
And coming into the cave we looked at everything.
The racks were laden with cheeses, and the pens were crowded
with lambs and kids; and each was penned apart,
the firstlings apart, the middle ones apart,
and the newborn apart. And all the vessels swam with whey,
pails and bowls, well-made, into which he milked.
There first my companions begged me with words
to take some of the cheeses and go back, and then
quickly, driving the kids and lambs out of the pens
to the swift ship, to sail over the salt water;
but I did not obey, though it would have been much better,
that I might see him myself, and see if he would give me guest-gifts.
Nor was he, appearing, to be lovely to my companions.
There we kindled a fire and sacrificed, and ourselves
taking some of the cheeses ate, and waited for him inside,
sitting, until he came back, shepherding. And he carried a mighty load
of dry wood, that it might be for his supper,
and throwing it down inside the cave he made a din;
and we, frightened, darted back into the recess of the cave.
And he drove his fat flocks into the wide cave,
all those that he milked, and left the males outside the door,
the rams and he-goats, outside the deep court.
Then he set on the door a great stone, lifting it on high,
massive; not twenty-two good
four-wheeled wagons could have moved it from the ground;
such a towering rock he set against the door.
And sitting he milked the ewes and bleating goats,
all in due order, and put under each her young.
At once then, having curdled half of the white milk,
he gathered it and put it in wicker baskets,
and the other half he stood in vessels, that it might be
for him to take and drink, and for his supper.
But when he had hurried through his labours,
then he kindled the fire and saw us, and asked us:
'Strangers, who are you? Whence do you sail the watery ways?
Is it on some business, or do you wander at random,
like pirates over the sea, who wander
staking their lives, bringing evil to men of other lands?'
So he spoke, and our dear heart was broken,
in fear of the heavy voice and the monster himself.
But even so I answered him with words and said:
'We are Achaeans, wandering from Troy,
driven by winds of all kinds over the great gulf of the sea,
longing for home, by another way, other paths
we have come; so, I suppose, Zeus wished to plan.
We declare that we are men of Agamemnon, son of Atreus,
whose fame now is greatest under heaven;
for so great a city he sacked, and destroyed many
people. But we have come, reaching your knees,
in case you would give a guest-gift or even otherwise
offer a present, which is the due of strangers.
But respect the gods, best of men; we are suppliants,
and Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and strangers,
the god of guests, who attends with revered strangers.'
So I spoke, and he at once answered me with a pitiless heart:
'You are foolish, stranger, or have come from afar,
who bid me either fear the gods or avoid them;
for the Cyclopes care nothing for aegis-bearing Zeus
nor for the blessed gods, since we are far stronger.
Nor would I, to avoid the hatred of Zeus, spare
you or your companions, unless my spirit bid me.
But tell me where you stopped your well-built ship when you came,
whether at the far end or near by, that I may know.'
So he spoke, testing me, but it did not escape me, who knew much,
and I answered him in turn with crafty words:
'My ship Poseidon the Earth-shaker broke,
casting it on the rocks at the boundaries of your land,
bringing it up to a headland; and the wind carried it from the sea;
but I with these escaped sheer destruction.'
So I spoke, and he answered me nothing with his pitiless heart,
but leaping up he threw his hands upon my companions,
and seizing two together, like puppies, dashed them
to the ground; and their brains flowed out onto the earth and wetted the ground.
Then cutting them limb from limb he prepared his supper;
and he ate like a mountain-bred lion, and left nothing,
entrails and flesh and marrowy bones.
And we, weeping, held up our hands to Zeus,
seeing the cruel deeds, and helplessness held our hearts.
But when the Cyclops had filled his great belly
eating man's flesh and drinking unmixed milk,
he lay inside the cave, stretched out among the sheep.
I planned in my great-hearted spirit
to go close, drawing my sharp sword from my thigh,
and stab him in the chest, where the midriff holds the liver,
feeling for the place with my hand; but another thought held me back.
For we too would have perished there by sheer destruction;
for we could not have pushed away with our hands
the mighty stone from the high doors, which he had set there.
So then, groaning, we waited for divine Dawn.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then he kindled the fire and milked his famous flocks,
all in due order, and put under each her young.
But when he had hurried through his labours,
again seizing two together he prepared his meal.
Having eaten, he drove his fat flocks out of the cave,
easily taking off the great stone; and then
he put it back, as if one were putting a lid on a quiver.
With much whistling the Cyclops turned his fat flocks to the mountain;
and I was left, devising evils,
if somehow I might take vengeance, and Athena grant me glory.
And this plan seemed best to me in my heart.
By the pen lay a great club of the Cyclops,
green olive-wood; he had cut it to carry
when dried. We, looking at it, judged it
to be as large as the mast of a black twenty-oared
broad freighter, which crosses the great gulf;
so great was its length, so great its thickness to look at.
From it I stood by and cut off about a fathom,
and set it down beside my companions, and bade them smooth it down;
and they made it even; and I stood by and sharpened
the tip, and at once took it and hardened it in the blazing fire.
And this I laid away well, hiding it under dung,
which lay in great abundance all over the cave;
and I bade the others cast lots,
which of them should dare, with me, lifting the stake,
to twist it in his eye, when sweet sleep came upon him.
And the lot fell on those whom I myself would have wished to choose,
four, and I was the fifth counted among them.
In the evening he came, shepherding his fair-fleeced flocks.
At once he drove his fat flocks into the wide cave,
all of them, and left none outside the deep court,
either suspecting something, or a god so bade.
Then he set the great stone on the door, lifting it on high,
and sitting he milked the ewes and bleating goats,
all in due order, and put under each her young.
But when he had hurried through his labours,
again seizing two together he prepared his supper.
Then I spoke to the Cyclops, standing near him,
holding an ivy-wood bowl of dark wine in my hands:
'Cyclops, here, drink wine, since you have eaten man's flesh,
that you may know what kind of drink this was, which our ship
had hidden. And I was bringing it to you as a libation, in case you would pity me
and send me home; but you rage past endurance.
Cruel one, how shall any other of many men come to you
hereafter, since you have not acted as is right?'
So I spoke, and he took it and drank it off; and he was terribly pleased
drinking the sweet drink, and asked me for a second time:
'Give me more, readily, and tell me your name
at once now, that I may give you a guest-gift in which you will rejoice;
for the grain-giving earth bears also for the Cyclopes
wine from rich clusters, and the rain of Zeus makes it grow;
but this is a rill of ambrosia and nectar.'
So he spoke, and again I gave him sparkling wine.
Three times I gave it, bringing it, and three times he drank it off in his folly.
And when the wine had gone round the Cyclops' wits,
then I addressed him with honeyed words:
'Cyclops, you ask me my famous name, and I
will tell you; and you give me a guest-gift, as you promised.
Nobody is my name; Nobody they call me,
my mother and father and all my other companions.'
So I spoke, and he at once answered me with a pitiless heart:
'Nobody I will eat last, after his companions,
and the others first; and this shall be your guest-gift.'
He spoke, and reclining he fell on his back, and then
lay with his thick neck bent aside, and sleep
that conquers all took him; and from his gullet wine gushed out
and morsels of men's flesh; and he belched, heavy with wine.
Then I thrust the stake into the deep ashes,
until it should be heated; and with words I encouraged
all my companions, lest any, fearing, hold back from me.
But when the olive stake was just about
to catch fire in the flame, green though it was, and glowed terribly,
then I brought it near from the fire, and my companions stood
around; and a god breathed great courage into us.
They took the olive stake, sharp at the point,
and thrust it into his eye; and I, leaning my weight from above,
twirled it, as when a man bores a ship's timber
with a drill, and those below shake it with a strap,
taking hold on each side, and it runs round continually.
So taking the fire-hardened stake in his eye
we twirled it, and the blood flowed round it, hot as it was.
All around his eyelids and brows the blast singed
from the burning eyeball, and its roots crackled in the fire.
As when a smith dips a great axe or adze
in cold water, hissing loudly,
tempering it; for that is the strength of iron;
so his eye hissed round the olive stake.
Terribly he gave a great cry, and the rock rang round,
and we, frightened, rushed back; and he pulled the stake
out of his eye, smeared with much blood.
Then he flung it from him with his hands, distraught,
and called loudly to the Cyclopes, who round about him
lived in caves along the windy heights.
And they, hearing the cry, came from this side and that,
and standing around the cave asked what troubled him:
'Why, Polyphemus, so distressed, have you cried out thus
through the ambrosial night and made us sleepless?
Surely no mortal is driving off your flocks against your will?
Surely no one is killing you by guile or by force?'
Then mighty Polyphemus spoke to them from the cave:
'My friends, Nobody is killing me by guile or by force.'
And they answered and spoke winged words:
'If then no one does you violence, being alone,
sickness from great Zeus is in no way possible to avoid;
but pray to your father, lord Poseidon.'
So they spoke and went away, and my dear heart laughed,
how my name deceived them and my blameless cunning.
But the Cyclops, groaning and in the pains of agony,
feeling with his hands, took the stone from the door,
and himself sat in the doorway with his arms outstretched,
in case he might catch anyone going out with the sheep;
for so, I suppose, he hoped in his mind that I was foolish.
But I was planning how things might turn out best,
if I could find some release from death for my companions and myself;
and I wove all kinds of tricks and plans,
as for a life; for a great evil was near.
And this plan seemed best to me in my heart.
There were male sheep, well-fed, thick-fleeced,
fine and large, having violet-dark wool;
these I silently bound together with well-twisted withies,
on which the Cyclops slept, the monster, who knew lawless ways,
taking three together; the middle one carried a man,
and the other two went on either side, keeping my companions safe.
Three sheep carried each man; but I—
for there was a ram, by far the best of all the flock,
taking him by the back, curled beneath his shaggy belly
I lay; and with my hands in the marvellous fleece
I clung, twisted, steadily with enduring heart.
So then, groaning, we waited for divine Dawn.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then the male sheep rushed out to pasture,
and the females bleated unmilked about the pens;
for their udders were bursting. And their master, in evil pains
worn down, felt the backs of all the sheep
as they stood upright; but the fool did not notice this,
that men were bound beneath the chests of the fleecy sheep.
Last of the flock the ram went toward the door,
burdened with his fleece and with me, thinking close thoughts.
And feeling him mighty Polyphemus said:
'Dear ram, why do you go through the cave thus
last of the flock? Never before have you gone left behind the sheep,
but far the first you pasture the tender flowers of the grass,
taking long strides, and first you reach the streams of the rivers,
and first you long to return to the stall
in the evening; now you are last of all. Surely you miss your master's
eye, which an evil man blinded
with his wretched companions, overcoming my wits with wine,
Nobody, who I say has not yet escaped destruction.
If only you had the same mind and could get a voice
to tell where he is skulking from my might;
then his brains would be dashed this way and that through the cave
against the ground, as he was struck, and my heart would
be eased of the woes which worthless Nobody gave me.'
So saying he sent the ram from him out of doors.
And when we had gone a little way from the cave and the court,
first I loosed myself from under the ram, and loosed my companions.
Quickly the long-shanked sheep, fat with tallow,
driving them often round about, we drove, until we came
to the ship. And welcome we appeared to our dear companions,
we who had escaped death, and they groaned, lamenting for the others.
But I would not allow it, and with a nod of my brows to each
forbade weeping, but bade them quickly throw the many
fair-fleeced sheep into the ship and sail over the salt water.
They quickly embarked and sat on the benches,
and sitting in order they struck the grey sea with oars.
But when I was as far off as a man's shout carries,
then I addressed the Cyclops with taunting words:
'Cyclops, so you were not going to eat the companions of a feeble man
in your hollow cave by main force.
And indeed evil deeds were going to overtake you,
cruel one, since you did not shrink from eating guests
in your own house; therefore Zeus and the other gods have punished you.'
So I spoke, and he was angered still more in his heart,
and breaking off the peak of a great mountain he hurled it,
and cast it down before the dark-prowed ship,
a little short; and it fell short of reaching the tip of the rudder,
and the sea was washed up as the rock came down;
and the back-flowing wave bore it quickly to the mainland,
a flood from the sea, and forced it to reach the land.
But I, taking in my hands a very long pole,
pushed her off, and urging my companions I bade them
fall to the oars, that we might escape from evil,
nodding with my head; and they fell forward and rowed.
But when we were twice as far, pressing through the sea,
then I addressed the Cyclops; and around me my companions
held me back with honeyed words from this side and that:
'Cruel one, why do you wish to provoke a savage man?
Who even now, throwing a missile into the sea, brought the ship
back to the land, and we thought we should perish there.
And if he had heard any one of us make a sound or speak,
he would have crushed our heads and the ship's timbers together,
throwing a jagged rock; so far does he hurl.'
So they spoke, but they did not persuade my great-hearted spirit,
and I answered him again with an angry heart:
'Cyclops, if anyone of mortal men
asks you about the unseemly blinding of your eye,
say that Odysseus, sacker of cities, blinded it,
the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.'
So I spoke, and he, groaning, answered me with a word:
'Oh dear, truly the oracles of old have come upon me.
There was here a seer, a good and great man,
Telemus, son of Eurymus, who excelled in prophecy
and grew old prophesying among the Cyclopes;
he told me that all this would be accomplished hereafter,
that I should lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus.
But I always expected some tall and handsome man
to come here, clothed in great strength;
and now one small and worthless and feeble
has blinded my eye, since he overcame me with wine.
But come here, Odysseus, that I may set before you guest-gifts
and urge the famous Earth-shaker to give you an escort;
for I am his son, and he declares himself my father.
And he himself will heal me, if he wishes, and no other
either of the blessed gods or of mortal men.'
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
'Would that I could deprive you of life and breath
and send you into the house of Hades,
as surely as not even the Earth-shaker will heal your eye.'
So I spoke, and then he prayed to lord Poseidon,
stretching out his hands to the starry heaven:
'Hear me, Poseidon earth-holder, dark-haired one;
if I am truly yours, and you declare yourself my father,
grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, may not come home,
the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.
But if it is his fate to see his friends and to reach
his well-built house and his native land,
let him come late and in evil plight, having lost all his companions,
in another's ship, and find troubles in his house.'
So he spoke praying, and the dark-haired god heard him.
And he again lifted a far larger stone,
and whirling it hurled it, and put into it measureless force,
and cast it down behind the dark-prowed ship,
a little short; and it fell short of reaching the tip of the rudder.
And the sea was washed up as the rock came down;
and the wave bore the ship forward, and forced it to reach the land.
But when we reached the island, where the other
well-benched ships stayed all together, and around them our companions
sat lamenting, always waiting for us,
coming there we ran our ship onto the sand,
and went out ourselves onto the shore of the sea.
And the flocks of the Cyclops, taking from the hollow ship,
we divided, that none might go off cheated of an equal share.
And the ram, to me alone, my well-greaved companions,
when the flocks were being divided, gave as a special portion; and him on the shore
to Zeus of the dark clouds, son of Cronos, who rules over all,
I sacrificed and burned the thigh-pieces; but he did not heed the offerings,
but pondered how all my well-benched ships
and my trusty companions might perish.
So then all day until the sun set
we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
when the sun set and darkness came on,
then we lay down on the shore of the sea.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then I urged on my companions and bade them
embark themselves and loose the stern cables;
they quickly embarked and sat on the benches,
and sitting in order they struck the grey sea with oars.
From there we sailed on, grieved at heart,
glad to escape death, having lost our dear companions.
